title: Convey, even one verse
hookLine: convey from me, even one verse, and in the same breath, don't lie about me
tomorrow: what made one teacher keep his seat in the mosque?

cards: Someone posts a verse over a photo of a sunset. Someone else replies: you're not a scholar, stay in your lane. Who's right?
Do you have to be an expert before you share? One short hadith seems to answer at once. Then, in the very same breath, it adds a warning, and people still weigh the two halves.

teach.h: CONVEY FROM ME, EVEN ONE VERSE.
teach.b: It's in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: convey from me, even if it's one aya, one verse.
And at the end of the same hadith: whoever lies about me on purpose, let him take his seat in the Fire. Two halves. Each has its defenders.
One view leans on the first half. Even one verse. You don't need a degree to pass on what you've truly learned.
The Prophet asked for it, and he set the bar low: one verse. A community where only experts speak goes quiet.

At its best, this side says: knowledge that isn't shared dies with the person who holds it. The other view leans on the second half. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words: "follow not that whereof thou hast no knowledge."
Passing on a hadith you half-remember, or an explanation you made up on the spot, isn't humility. It can put words in the Prophet's mouth.

teach.h: SIDE TWO: A WRONG WORD SPREADS.
teach.b: At its best, this side says: a wrong word travels faster than a right one, and it's hard to call back.
The hadith itself keeps both halves in one breath. Share. Don't invent.

how: Muslims share verses and hadith with family, friends and online, often quoting this hadith; teachers also urge checking a hadith's source before passing it on.

o: to explain a text the way an expert would
to pass on what you've received to others
to persuade someone to change religion

games.q: what's inside the debate — tap the pairs.
p: follow not what you don't know

s: in Islam, only scholars are allowed to pass on a verse
the Prophet said: convey from me, even one verse.
the hadith that says 'even one verse' also warns against lying about the Prophet
both halves sit in the same hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari.
'even one verse' means any explanation you like is fine to share
17:36: follow not that whereof thou hast no knowledge.

games.q: you lean toward the sharing side: everyone should pass on what they know. what's the strongest case for the careful side?
o: a wrong word about the Prophet spreads fast and is hard to call back.
sharing a verse makes you look like a show-off, and that spoils it.
the Qur'an forbids anyone but scholars from quoting it in public.
games.why: the careful side rests on the hadith's own second half and on 17:36: don't follow what you don't know. it isn't against sharing; it's against inventing.

practice: Choose one line you know well and trust: a verse, a short surah, even just bismillah. Check that you have it exactly, then say it once, slowly, out loud. Let it sit in the quiet after.

wordCard.voice: Convey: to pass on what you've received. In the hadith, even one verse is enough to count, as long as it's passed on true.

orig.note: Arabic: 'convey from me', the hadith's opening words.

carryVoice: Pocket this: even one verse, as long as it's the real one. Catch you tomorrow.
